<reason>PRO built a tight case on control, foreseeability, and cheapest-cost-avoider logic, consistently framed as "more, not all" responsibility, and kept the uncompensated pedestrian at the center. CON fought well with a genuine fault-versus-funding distinction, the GPS-drift/sidewalk-detection problem, and the car-substitution weighing, and landed a real hit when PRO retreated to a zone-wide speed cap. But under PRO's Q1 pressure CON conceded a company-administered, per-ride-funded insurance pool, which PRO credibly framed as the motion renamed; CON's "it's the rider's money" reply is thin since all liability costs pass through to riders anyway. CON's closing kinetic-energy flip was clever but relied on inflating PRO's "half a block" cap into "throttle a district" and on a speculative substitution chain PRO had already labeled as preferring rider convenience over pedestrian safety. CON also had two clipped turns and PRO one stray misreference; net, PRO left the cleaner, more motion-faithful path to a vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A3.1 pressure question ("who compensates her?") forced CON's B4.1 no-fault pool, which PRO's A5.1 turned into a concession that the operator collects, administers, and pays out for sidewalk injuries; CON's B5.1 "rider's money, no fault finding" response could not fully undo that shift.</best_rebuttal>
